source_read: PDF PDFs/Alcohol/Schuckit_2014_WithdrawalDelirium.pdf, the version of record, N Engl J Med 2014;371(22):2109–2113: all 5 pages read (text extraction with -layout); pp. 2110, 2111 and 2112, whose two columns the extraction interleaves, were read on pages rendered at 110 dpi, including Tables 1 and 2 and the Conclusions; Table 3 (regimens) read but not recorded; conflict-of-interest line and all 33 references read. No supplement; the NEJM disclosure forms were not read.

claims.overstatement: None. The claim attributes every figure to the review, says the figures are second-hand and keeps the hospital denominators ('in hospital for alcohol withdrawal', 'hospital patients with withdrawal delirium'). 'Signs that delirium is more likely' matches the review's 'predicted by' (no effect sizes are given, and the claim gives none). 'Without the designs or settings of its sources' slightly understates the review, which does name the setting of the 3 to 5% and 1 to 4% figures (hospitalized patients) and says chart reviews give higher rates, but it gives no designs, sample sizes or periods, so the phrase is fair.
claims.note: Numbers checked against the source, all the same: about 50% with withdrawal symptoms and 3 to 5% of them with seizures, delirium or both (p. 2109, cited to DSM-5); 3 to 5% of patients hospitalized for withdrawal meeting the criteria; onset about 3 days after withdrawal symptoms; 1 to 8 days or more, usually 2 or 3; about 1 to 4% case fatality among hospitalized patients; CIWA-Ar above 15, systolic pressure above 150 mm Hg, pulse above 100; recent withdrawal seizures in 20% of people with delirium (all p. 2110); DSM-5 criteria, two of eight symptoms (Table 2, p. 2111); no conflict of interest reported and no funding statement (p. 2113). No editors' calculation from this source. Suggested addition (qualifier the claim leaves out): the review itself says prevalence is hard to establish because clinicians differ in how closely they follow the criteria and rates depend on the care setting (outpatient, general medical or psychiatric ward, intensive care), and that retrospective chart reviews by general clinicians give higher but less reliable rates (p. 2110). The two 3 to 5% ranges are different quantities (p. 2109: seizures, delirium or both, among everyone with an alcohol use disorder who has withdrawal symptoms; p. 2110: delirium among patients hospitalized for withdrawal); the claim keeps them apart correctly. The p. 2109 figure is the only one not limited to hospital patients, which fits the claim's closing caveat because it is relayed from DSM-5, not measured. The CIWA-Ar band above 15 is also in the Table 1 footnote (p. 2110) as severe withdrawal carrying a danger of seizures, delirium or both. Predictor sources include two retrospective studies (refs 13 and 16, by their titles) and the author's own 1995 study (ref 17).

anchors.locator: States of Alcohol Withdrawal › Withdrawal Delirium (Delirium Tremens), 1st paragraph (p. 2110); Table 2 and its footnote (p. 2111)
anchors.extracted: Definition, following DSM-5 (ref 1): withdrawal delirium is delirium (a rapid-onset, fluctuating disturbance of attention and cognition, sometimes with hallucinations) plus alcohol withdrawal. Table 2: withdrawal = stopping or reducing heavy and prolonged use plus at least 2 of 8 symptoms (autonomic hyperactivity, hand tremor, insomnia, nausea or vomiting, transient hallucinations or illusions, psychomotor agitation, anxiety, generalized tonic–clonic seizures); delirium = reduced attention and awareness, a disturbance of attention, awareness, memory, orientation, language, visuospatial ability or perception that is a change from normal and fluctuates during the day, and no coma or other evolving neurocognitive disorder. Footnote: meeting both sets of criteria = withdrawal delirium.

anchors.locator: Opening section (before States of Alcohol Withdrawal), 2nd paragraph
anchors.extracted: About 50% of people with an alcohol use disorder have withdrawal symptoms when they cut down or stop; in 3 to 5% of these, grand mal convulsions, delirium or both develop. Single citation: DSM-5 (ref 1); no study design, setting or period given.

anchors.locator: States of Alcohol Withdrawal › Withdrawal Delirium (Delirium Tremens), 1st paragraph
anchors.extracted: Prevalence hard to determine because clinicians differ in how well they follow the criteria; rates depend on whether patients were treated as outpatients, general medical or psychiatric inpatients, or in intensive care. Most studies estimate that 3 to 5% of patients hospitalized for alcohol withdrawal meet the criteria for withdrawal delirium (refs 7, 10, 11). Retrospective chart reviews based on general clinicians' diagnoses give higher but less reliable rates.

anchors.locator: States of Alcohol Withdrawal › Withdrawal Delirium (Delirium Tremens), 2nd paragraph
anchors.extracted: Onset usually about 3 days after withdrawal symptoms appear; lasts 1 to 8 days or more, usually 2 or 3 (refs 7, 9, 12). About 1 to 4% of hospitalized patients with withdrawal delirium die; the author says the rate could be reduced by appropriate, timely diagnosis and adequate treatment (refs 7, 9, 11, 13; no size of reduction given). Death usually from hyperthermia, cardiac arrhythmias, complications of withdrawal seizures or concomitant medical disorders (refs 14, 15).

anchors.locator: States of Alcohol Withdrawal › Withdrawal Delirium (Delirium Tremens), 3rd paragraph; Table 1 footnote
anchors.extracted: Predictors of delirium in withdrawal (no effect sizes): CIWA-Ar above 15, especially with systolic blood pressure above 150 mm Hg or pulse above 100 a minute; recent withdrawal seizures (seen in 20% of people with delirium); prior withdrawal delirium or seizures; older age; recent misuse of other depressants; concomitant medical problems, including low potassium, magnesium or both, low platelets, and respiratory, cardiac or gastrointestinal disease (refs 7, 10, 11, 13, 16, 17). Table 1 footnote: CIWA-Ar totals 0 to 67; above 15 = severe withdrawal with a danger of grand mal seizures, delirium or both.
No potential conflict of interest relevant to the article was reported; disclosure forms are on NEJM.org (not read). The article carries no funding statement.

claims.overstatement: None for the sentence drawn from this source.
claims.note: The sentence 'nine controlled trials from 1959 to 1978 and later uncontrolled studies' matches pp. 2110–2111. Three precisions the editor may want: (1) the count is relayed from a 2004 review (ref 9: Mayo-Smith et al., Arch Intern Med 2004;164:1405–12, the ASAM guideline on withdrawal delirium), a different paper from the 1997 JAMA meta-analysis this claim also cites, so the figure is third-hand; (2) the review calls the nine 'prospective, controlled', not randomized or double-blind, and says few double-blind, controlled, prospective trials exist; (3) the later studies were found by a PubMed search whose terms and dates are not given. The review's own summary of the evidence could be added as a qualifier: data on the most effective care for withdrawal delirium are lacking, and the treatment amounts it describes are approximations based on uncontrolled studies (Conclusions, p. 2112). Consistent with other parts of the claim: no single benzodiazepine has been shown superior to another (p. 2111), the alternatives are less well studied and carry additional dangers (p. 2112), and antipsychotics can prolong the QT interval and make seizures more likely (p. 2112), in line with the phenothiazine results the claim takes from Mayo-Smith (1997). No numbers from this source other than 9, 1959 and 1978, all checked. The claim contains no dose or regimen; I have recorded none from Table 3.

anchors.locator: Treatment of Withdrawal Delirium, 1st paragraph (begins p. 2110, continues p. 2111)
anchors.extracted: Few double-blind, controlled, prospective treatment trials exist (author suggests low prevalence, high costs and lack of commercial incentive as possible reasons). The best evidence is a 2004 review (ref 9, Mayo-Smith et al., 2004) of nine prospective, controlled trials conducted between 1959 and 1978, plus later noncontrolled studies identified in a PubMed search (terms, dates not given).

anchors.locator: Treatment of Withdrawal Delirium, 4th paragraph (p. 2111) and 6th paragraph (p. 2112); Conclusions (p. 2112)
anchors.extracted: Benzodiazepines are the mainstay; no single drug of the class has been shown superior to another. Alternative and adjunctive drugs have not been studied as well as benzodiazepines and carry additional dangers with few advantages for most patients; antipsychotics can prolong the QT interval and increase the likelihood of seizures. Conclusions: all amounts described are approximations based on uncontrolled studies, and data on the most effective care are lacking.

key_findings.note: Checked on p. 2109: 20% of men and 10% of women; more than 20% of patients in most medical settings; about 50% with withdrawal symptoms, 3 to 5% of them with seizures, delirium or both; the decade-of-life sentence has no reference marker of its own.
Within 8 hours, peak about 72 hours, markedly reduced by days 5 to 7 (p. 2109). The paragraph's symptom list is also cited to DSM-5 (ref 1) besides refs 4 to 7.
Table 1 and footnote (p. 2110): 9 items 0 to 7 plus 1 item 0 to 4, totals 0 to 67 (9 × 7 + 4 = 67), bands below 8, 8 to 15, above 15, alternative cut-off 10; data from Kosten and O'Connor (ref 4).

Finding confirmed. The note's 'reviews and small or uncontrolled studies' is slightly loose: by their titles, refs 26 and 27 are placebo-controlled trials (ref 26 a randomized multicentre pilot) and ref 25 a comparison of two treatments, all in uncomplicated withdrawal rather than in withdrawal delirium; the note's point that no results of these studies are given stands.

reporting_issues.note: Same finding in my blind reading; the claim keeps the two quantities apart.
The reference list (p. 2113) has refs 4 (Kosten and O'Connor) and 8 (Williams et al., a comparison of rating scales); no Sullivan et al. CIWA-Ar development paper.

risk_of_bias.note: Editors' narrative-review checklist; overall high from the search-and-selection domain. I agree with each domain.

interpretation_gap.note: Minor: the review is candid that the treatment evidence is weak.

missed: Nothing important. Small point for the card's cannot_establish and the claim: the review does give the setting of its 3 to 5% and 1 to 4% figures (hospitalized patients), though not the designs, sizes or periods of the studies behind them (p. 2110).
